title: Three naive Bayes approaches for discrimination-free classification
abstract: In this paper, we investigate how to modify the naive Bayes classifier in order to perform classification that is restricted to be independent with respect to a given sensitive attribute. Such independency restrictions occur naturally when the decision process leading to the labels in the data-set was biased; e.g., due to gender or racial discrimination. This setting is motivated by many cases in which there exist laws that disallow a decision that is partly based on discrimination. Naive application of machine learning techniques would result in huge fines for companies. We present three approaches for making the naive Bayes classifier discrimination-free: (i) modifying the probability of the decision being positive, (ii) training one model for every sensitive attribute value and balancing them, and (iii) adding a latent variable to the Bayesian model that represents the unbiased label and optimizing the model parameters for likelihood using expectation maximization. We present experiments for the three approaches on both artificial and real-life data.

claims.text: Removing the sensitive attribute from training data fails to prevent indirect discrimination due to correlations with other attributes.
The 2 naive Bayes models approach achieves zero discrimination while maintaining high classification accuracy on the census income dataset.
The 2 naive Bayes models approach exhibits lower dependency on the sensitive attribute than the modified naive Bayes method when marginalizing over the sensitive attribute.
Expectation Maximization on the latent variable model converges on average to a non-zero discrimination assignment on synthetic data.
Stopping EM early when discrimination drops below 0.01 yields higher classification accuracy than allowing EM to converge to a local likelihood optimum.

limitations.text: The proposed naive Bayes approaches do not natively support continuous numerical attributes and require discretization and bin pooling prior to training.
Expectation Maximization on the latent variable model converges to local likelihood optima that do not correspond to zero discrimination and exhibits high variance across runs.
The latent variable model assumes uniform random discrimination and complete independence between latent true labels and sensitive attributes, which may simplify actual discrimination mechanisms.
Simply removing the sensitive attribute from training datasets fails to eliminate indirect discrimination caused by correlated features.

future_work.text: Extend the discrimination notion to conditional discrimination, permitting dependency when explained by valid non-sensitive attributes.
Extend discrimination-free Bayesian classification algorithms to handle numerical sensitive attributes.
Explore alternative graphical model structures, including inserting decision trees or reversing dependency direction relative to the sensitive attribute.
Investigate the mathematical reasons behind the poor convergence behavior of Expectation Maximization on synthetic datasets.

methodologies.name: Modified Naive Bayes (Algorithm 1)
methodologies.description: Modifies conditional probability P(C|S) in a post-processing loop to eliminate discrimination while attempting to preserve the total number of assigned positive class labels.

methodologies.name: 2 Naive Bayes Models
methodologies.description: Splits the training dataset by sensitive attribute values into two separate naive Bayes models and balances predictions by adjusting P(C|S).

methodologies.name: Latent Variable Model with Expectation Maximization
methodologies.description: Introduces an unobserved binary latent variable representing discrimination-free true labels and estimates parameters via Expectation Maximization, optionally leveraging pre-computed prior distributions.
conditions: Latent label independent of sensitive attribute
